title: Phase-Field Modeling of Liquid Phases with Ordering
abstract: A strong negative enthalpy of mixing can lead to ordering in liquid solutions. To describe ordering in liquids, different thermodynamic descriptions of liquid phases have been developed in the CALPHAD approach, including the associate model and the modified quasichemical model. In this study, we show that the key to directly incorporate these liquid phase models and their corresponding CALPHAD-type free energy formulations in phase-field simulations, is to identify the internal processes and to properly define the internal thermodynamic variables. The free energy of the liquid phase can then be converted to a function of component compositions and internal variables, and the evolution of the internal variables will be determined via Allen-Cahn-type relaxation equations. We demonstrate this modeling strategy using the formation of stoichiometric phases from liquid phases in Na-Sb and Na-Sn systems. This study will pave the way for predicting microstructure evolution in liquids with ordering using phase-field simulations.
summary: This work establishes a rigorous theoretical framework to integrate complex thermodynamic descriptions of liquid ordering, such as the MQMPA model, into phase-field simulations. By defining Internal Process Order Parameters (IPOPs) and evolving them via Allen-Cahn equations, the authors enable the prediction of microstructure evolution in liquid alloys with strong ordering tendencies. This advances the predictive capability of computational materials science for systems relevant to energy storage.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing a unified framework to incorporate complex, composition-dependent thermodynamic descriptions of liquid ordering (like Associate or MQMPA models) directly into phase-field simulations.
main_result: The authors successfully propose a methodology where internal degrees of freedom related to ordering are modeled as Internal Process Order Parameters (IPOPs), whose evolution is governed by Allen-Cahn equations coupled to standard phase-field dynamics.
method: The approach involves identifying internal thermodynamic variables, formulating the free energy density based on these variables, and solving coupled partial differential equations (Allen-Cahn for IPOPs, diffusion equations for compositions).
model_or_system: The study focuses on binary liquid A-B systems (e.g., Na-Sb, Na-Sn) exhibiting Short-Range Ordering (SRO) due to negative enthalpy of mixing. The liquid phase thermodynamics are described using advanced CALPHAD models like the Associate Model or the Modified Quasichemical Model (MQMPA).
key_observables: Internal Process Order Parameters (IPOPs, $\xi$), phase order parameter ($\eta$), component compositions ($x_B$), and the resulting microstructure evolution.
important_parameters: Negative enthalpy of mixing ($\Delta H_{	ext{mix}}$), temperature (e.g., 1000 K, 600 K), and kinetic coefficients ($L_{\xi}$).
main_assumptions: The evolution of the IPOP ($\xi$) is assumed to be much faster than the evolution of composition ($x_B$), allowing for iterative solution schemes. Specific approximations are made for configurational entropy in the MQMPA model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase-field model framework, showing IPOP evolution in Na-Sb and Na-Sn liquids converging to equilibrium, and detailing the evolution of phase order parameters and compositions during solidification.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the need to couple liquid ordering thermodynamics to phase-field models. It details the mathematical formulation for both the Associate and MQMPA models, deriving the coupled evolution equations. Finally, it validates this framework through simulations of Na-Sb and Na-Sn systems.
why_interesting: While the primary focus is materials thermodynamics, the use of Allen-Cahn equations to model the relaxation of internal degrees of freedom (IPOPs) is a general technique for describing non-equilibrium phase transitions, which has parallels in modeling complex quantum many-body dynamics.
